label: Losing a tooth

what_happens.title: Why teeth get wobbly
goals: Baby teeth make room for big teeth
A wobbly tooth gets looser a little each day
It comes out when it is ready
what_happens.parentSkill: Show your child a picture of baby teeth and grown-up teeth and explain that the new tooth pushes from below.

who_is_there.title: Who helps with a wobbly tooth
goals: [[GROWNUP]] is there to help and to look
The dentist checks teeth and knows about wobbly ones
Friends at school lose teeth too
who_is_there.parentSkill: Tell your child about your own first lost tooth, or ask a grandparent to tell theirs.

what_i_do.title: What I do with a wobbly tooth
goals: When it comes out: rinse, hold a tissue, keep the tooth
what_i_do.parentSkill: Agree on a plan for when the tooth falls out: rinse, tissue, and a small box or envelope for the tooth.

if_scared.title: If the wobbly tooth feels strange
goals: It can feel strange, sore or tickly
A little blood is normal and stops soon
Calm tools: slow breaths, cool water, a hug
if_scared.parentSkill: Name the feeling and the fact: 'It feels strange. A little blood is normal, and it stops soon.'

rehearsal.title: Let's practise the tooth plan
goals: Say the tooth plan out loud: rinse, tissue, box
Practise with a toy that has a pretend wobbly tooth
End with a big smile in the mirror
rehearsal.parentSkill: Let your child be the dentist and check a toy's wobbly tooth, then switch roles.

steps: Wiggle it gently with a clean finger or the tongue
Keep eating soft and crunchy food as usual
The tooth gets looser day by day
The tooth comes out, maybe while eating or brushing
Rinse the mouth with water and hold a tissue on the gap
Keep the tooth safe and look at the new gap in the mirror
sensory: a wiggly feeling when the tongue pushes the tooth
a tiny taste of metal when it comes out
a little bit of blood on a tissue
a soft, squishy gap where the tooth was
a whistle when talking through the gap
the hard edge of a new tooth coming in
honestyNotes: A wobbly tooth can feel sore or strange, and there may be a little blood when it comes out. Never say it will feel like nothing; say it can sting for a moment and stops soon. Never force a tooth out. If a family tradition (a tooth fairy or another) is used, let the parent decide what to say.

fallbackAnswer: A wobbly tooth can feel sore, and it may sting for a moment when it comes out.
Then it stops, and cool water helps.
Maybe a little, and that is normal.
A clean tissue on the gap helps it stop soon.
A new big tooth is growing underneath and pushes the baby tooth out.
It means you are growing.
No need to pull hard. You can wiggle it gently, and it comes out when it is ready.
If it is very loose, [[GROWNUP]] can help.
A baby tooth is tiny, and if you swallow it, it just passes through your body.
It is okay, and you can still tell everyone you lost a tooth.

questionButtons.text: When does the new tooth come?
fallbackAnswer: The new tooth often peeks through in a few weeks, sometimes a bit longer.
You can check in the mirror every week.

questionButtons.text: What if it falls out at school?
fallbackAnswer: Tell your teacher. Teachers help with lost teeth all the time.
They can give you a tissue and an envelope for the tooth.

questionButtons.text: Will I look funny with a gap?
fallbackAnswer: You will have a gap smile, like lots of kids your age.
Gaps are a sign you are growing, and the new tooth will fill it.
Yes. You can eat on the other side if the tooth feels sore.
Crunchy apples can even help it along.

questionButtons.text: What do we do with my tooth?
fallbackAnswer: [[GROWNUP]] will tell you what our family does with lost teeth.
Some families keep them in a box, and some have a special story about them.

questionButtons.text: Do I need to see the dentist?
fallbackAnswer: Usually not for a wobbly tooth. The dentist checks your teeth at your normal check-up.
If it is very sore, the dentist can help.

techniques.label: Gentle wiggles
techniques.how: Wiggle the tooth gently with the tongue, never pull hard.

techniques.label: The tooth plan
techniques.how: Rinse, tissue, box, smile: say the plan together so a surprise tooth is easy.

techniques.label: Cool water rinse
techniques.how: Rinse the mouth with cool water when the tooth comes out.

techniques.label: A tooth box
techniques.how: Pick a little box or envelope for the tooth before it comes out.

techniques.label: Mirror check
techniques.how: Look at the wobbly tooth and the gap in the mirror together.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

techniques.label: Looking away from the tissue
techniques.how: Let your child look away from the tissue if blood feels yucky.

techniques.label: Telling the teacher
techniques.how: Tell the teacher about the wobbly tooth and pack a small envelope.

techniques.label: A gap smile photo
techniques.how: Take a photo of the new gap smile for the family.

ritual: Big gap smile in the mirror

sentences.text: [[CHILD]] has a wobbly tooth.
It moves a little when the tongue pushes it.
This is a baby tooth, the kind every child has.
Under it, a new big tooth is growing.
The big tooth pushes up slowly, and the baby tooth gets looser.
Before bed, here is a story about a little squirrel called Pip.
Pip had a front tooth that went wiggle, wiggle.
Pip felt worried and asked Grandma Squirrel, is my tooth broken?
Grandma smiled and said, no, little one, it is getting ready.
A new strong tooth is growing underneath, just right for big nuts.
Every day, Pip wiggled the tooth gently with a tongue.
First it moved a tiny bit, then a little more, then a lot.
One morning Pip bit a soft berry, and pop, out came the tooth.
There was a gap, and Pip looked in a puddle and grinned.
Soon the new tooth came, step by step.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
First it wiggles a tiny bit, then a bit more each day.
Next it hangs on by a little thread.
Last, one day, it comes out, maybe while eating an apple or brushing teeth.
Then there is a gap, and soon the new tooth peeks through.

Most kids lose their first baby tooth around age six, and they keep losing them until about twelve.
The roots of a baby tooth slowly melt away as the adult tooth pushes up, so the tooth stays only in the gum.
That is why it gets wobbly and then comes out.
Adult teeth are bigger and need to last a whole life.
[[CHILD]] can keep them strong by brushing twice a day.
Dentists keep an eye on how adult teeth come in, because sometimes a new tooth grows behind a baby tooth that has not fallen out yet.
That is called a shark tooth, and it is common.
If a tooth is very sore or a new tooth looks crooked, the dentist can help.
[[CHILD]] can ask the dentist any question about teeth.
[[CHILD]] can tell [[GROWNUP]] if anything feels strange.
A loose tooth can come out at school, at dinner or even in sleep, and that is fine.
The gap may bleed a little for a few minutes, and pressing a clean tissue on it helps it stop.
If the tooth gets swallowed, it is tiny and simply passes through the body.
Brushing gently keeps the gap clean while the new tooth grows.
[[CHILD]] can pack a small tooth envelope for school, just in case.
It is normal to feel uneasy about blood, even a little.
Baby tooth gaps bleed only a tiny bit because the root has already melted away.
The sting is short, and most kids say it felt less than they expected.
If a tooth is sore for many days, the dentist can check it.
[[CHILD]] can look away from the tissue and breathe out slowly if blood feels yucky.
A plan makes surprises easier.
[[CHILD]] can decide where the tooth box lives and what to do if the tooth comes out at school.
Some kids keep a tooth diary with the date of each lost tooth and a picture of the gap.
Some families have a tooth fairy tradition, and some do not, and both are fine.
[[CHILD]] can make a tooth chart and colour each tooth as it comes out.
